# Genesis Apocryphon Column 2 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** 1QapGen (Cave 1), Col. 2 | **Condition:** Fragmentary; best-preserved early column

---

**2:1** Then I, Lamech, was afraid and I went to Bitenosh my wife [...]

**2:2** [...] and I said to her:

**2:3** Swear to me by the Most High, by the Lord of Greatness, by the King of all the Ages,

**2:4** [...] the sons of heaven, that you will tell me everything in truth,

**2:5** whether [...] you will tell me without falsehood.

**2:6** [...] swear to me [...] not with deception [...]

**2:7** [...tell me everything] truthfully [...] and not in anger

**2:8** [...] whether this child is from the Watchers of Heaven

**2:9** [...] or from the holy ones [...] or from the Nephilim

**2:10** [...] tell me everything [...] truthfully [...]

**2:11** Then Bitenosh my wife spoke to me with great vehemence

**2:12** and [...] she wept and said: O my lord and my brother,

**2:13** remember my pleasure; the time of love

**2:14** and the gasping of my breath within my breast.

**2:15** I tell you everything truthfully.

**2:16** [...]

**2:17** [...] my heart then changed greatly within me

**2:18** [...] and when Bitenosh my wife saw that my countenance had changed

**2:19** [...] then she restrained her anger and spoke to me and said:

**2:20** O my lord and my brother, remember my pleasure.

**2:21** I swear to you by the Great Holy One, by the King of the Heavens

**2:22** [...] that from you is this seed and from you is this conception

**2:23** and from you is the planting of this fruit.

**2:24** It is not from any stranger, and not from any Watcher,

**2:25** and not from any of the sons of heaven.

**2:26** [...] why is your countenance thus changed and disfigured [...]

---

*SOPHIA notes: Column 2 consensus follows LOGOS for most renderings, with EMET's precision in preserving the oath formulae. PNEUMA's dynamic expansions ("overcome with fear," "fierce intensity," "gasped with pleasure") were judged too interpretive for fragmentary text. The divine titles are preserved in their formal Aramaic-derived forms. "Planting of this fruit" is retained as a faithful and evocative rendering of the Aramaic conception idiom.*
